$comment: The map: what this app is made of, and where you touch it to change each part.
Same rule as docs/validation/ledger.json — one source, several renderers. This file
is the only place the map is written; `make map` prints it, `make map FEATURE=<id>`
prints one feature, and the /extend skill drives a session from it. Never restate a
feature's entrypoints anywhere else; point at the id.
WHY THIS IS JSON AND NOT PROSE, and why it holds symbols instead of line numbers:
an orientation doc is only worth reading if it is true, and the usual ones rot
silently — a file gets renamed, a function moves, and the map keeps confidently
pointing at nothing. scripts/gate-map.mjs runs in CI and in the pre-commit hook: it
opens every file listed here and checks that every `symbol` still literally appears
in it. A rename fails the build on the commit that does the renaming, naming the map
entry to update. Line numbers are what rots fastest, so they are never stored — the
renderer computes them at print time, so what you read is always where it is now.
FIELDS
id         kebab-case, stable; what you pass to `make map FEATURE=`.
what       one line, in the user's terms, not the code's.
layer      L1 core | L2 web | L3 etl | gate — where this feature's weight sits.
entry      the ordered path through the code. Read them top to bottom and you have
the feature. `file` + `symbol` (checked) + `note` (why you'd stop here).
extend     ordered steps for the most common change to this feature. Written as
what to do, not what exists.
gates      what will judge the change — run these before you believe it works.
seeAlso    ids of features that will notice if you change this one.
ADDING A FEATURE: add an entry here. The gate does not require one per file, and it
should not — a map that lists everything is an `ls`. List what someone arriving
cold would otherwise have to find by grep.

features.what: Tap an ayah on the page, or drag a marquee across several, and see amber marker swipes laid over them.

entry.note: The one decision the whole surface rests on: is this pointer a pan, a pinch, a tap, or a marquee? Everything downstream is a consequence. TAP_SLOP_PX and LONG_PRESS_MS are the thresholds a finger is judged by.
Screen point → ayah key, via the polygon manifest. The adapter between geometry and scripture; nothing above this layer knows what a polygon is.

Owns #hifth-overlay and every mark drawn in it. Framework-free and imperative on purpose — React must not re-render the stage. If you are adding a new kind of highlight, it is a StyleToken here, not a component. `paint` is where a style becomes either marker swipes or a cloned shape.

Why the highlight looks like a pen and not a box. Every ayah's hit area is a run of axis-aligned rectangles, one per line it occupies; this turns each into a band along the line's middle. It is a parser with a fallback, not an assumption — it returns null on any geometry it does not fully recognise and the Highlighter clones the shape instead, so an unfamiliar page degrades to the old box rather than to nothing. Loop 4b was the test of that: 601 pages arrived at once from the same upstream, and the fallback is still there for the edition that does not come from it.

The swipe branch is also the whole contract with the wipe animation, and none of it is visible. A `<line>` renders identically whichever end you write first, so the order of x1/x2 here is the only thing deciding which way the ink travels — right to left, because that is where a pen meets Arabic, and a backwards wipe would look subtly wrong to a reader and correct to everyone else. `--hl-len` and `--hl-i` are the two numbers CSS cannot work out for itself: a dash pattern must be told the stroke's length (`100%` on a line is the viewport, not the line) and which line of the ayah this is, so line 2 starts after line 1.
The React boundary. Binds @use-gesture to the surface, hands events to pointerIntent, and calls the Highlighter imperatively. The only file where the two worlds touch.

extend: Add the intent to `PointerIntent` and teach `pointerIntent`/`nextIntent` when to return it — with a unit test in gestures.test.ts first, because this is pure and cheap to pin.

If it draws something new, add a `StyleToken` and its branch in the Highlighter, then a CSS custom property in apps/web/src/styles/tokens.css. Decide whether it is ink: if so add it to `INKED` and give it an `--ink-*` token, because the ink rules blend with `multiply` and the alpha washes are tuned for compositing over — the two families are not interchangeable.
Wire it in PageStage. Resist adding state to React that the Highlighter already owns.

If it is inked it inherits the wipe, so it must emit `--hl-len` and `--hl-i` per element or it will draw solid and unanimated — the deliberate fallback, not a bug, but not the pen either. A motion rule that also sets the `animation` shorthand has to say which of the two renderings it is for: `.hl-sel.pulse` outranks `.hl-ink`, which is why the pulse carries `:not(.hl-ink)`.

Add a golden row if it changes pixels — see the `golden-images` feature. Note that a wipe is not pixels: Playwright fast-forwards finite animations to completion, so the goldens see the finished stroke and cannot see the wipe at all. Anything about how a mark arrives has to be a unit test on what the Highlighter wrote.

features.what: From a selected ayah, jump to the mutashabihat that resemble it — the reason this app exists.

entry.note: Loads and caches the per-surah edge shards from public/assets/adj/. Start here to understand what an edge IS.
Edges → rail chips, grouped by direction. `orderForHifz` beside it is the ranking a memoriser actually wants, which is not the ranking the data arrives in.

What a word run does to the edge list, and the reason it returns THREE outcomes rather than two. `about` is the edges whose span overlaps the run; `excluded` counts the ones that name words elsewhere in the ayah; `unplaced` is the edges that name no words at all — 15% of them, because a span is only emitted when the longest shared run occurs in exactly one place on both sides. Folding `unplaced` into either of the others would be a claim the data does not make. `Adjacency.hopsForWords` is the same thing keyed by a `<ayah>#w3-7` run, and it holds no root shards, so a caller who wants shared-root edges judged must pass `options.roots` — see `root-lens`.
The chips down the side. Arabic-Indic digits throughout, including in aria-labels — a sighted reader seeing ٣ and a screen-reader user hearing 'three' is a defect, and one the aria snapshots caught.
The chip's expansion: the destinations, and the diff against the current ayah.

The cross-page jump itself, and the case that is easy to get wrong: the destination is on another page, so the page must mount before the wash can land. `navigatedRef` is what stops an in-flight fetch from stomping a deep link that already arrived.

Where the hop lands. Scale SVG user units to px, put the target bbox's centre on the stage's centre — then `clampView` beside it decides whether the page may actually go there. Centring is a request, not a right: an ayah 40 px from the foot of the page can only be centred by dragging the page half a screen past its own end, and the reader is then looking at a margin. `holdAxis` is the whole rule in two regimes — a page bigger than the stage may roam over its overhang and no further; a page smaller than it has exactly one honest position, the middle.

The single choke point every hop, tween, drag and pinch writes through, which is why the clamp lives here and not on the hop's target: a lerp between two legal views passes through a zoom belonging to neither, and a drag after a correct landing would otherwise shove the page into the void. `measureFit` caches the stage/page box per gesture rather than per frame — reading layout inside a RAF tween is a read straight after a write to the element being measured, the forced-synchronous-layout shape the perf budget exists to keep out.
Where you have been. The hop is only useful if you can get back.

extend: New edge kind: add it to `EDGE_TYPES` in adjacency.ts and give it a status. `isActiveEdgeType` is what keeps a provisional kind out of the UI while its data is still being audited.
Emit it from packages/etl/scripts/build-adjacency.mjs, then re-run `make etl` — CI diffs the committed shards against a fresh ETL run, so a non-deterministic change fails the build.
If a human has ruled on specific edges, they belong in the curated set, not the dataset — gate:verified-edges enforces that a 'correct' edge still ships and a 'wrong' one stays gone, forever.
Check the shard budget in the ETL output; the largest shard is printed on every run.

Changing where a hop lands is `frameBboxToView`, and any *new* write to the host transform must go through `applyTransform` — a path that sets `host.style.transform` itself is a path the clamp cannot see. apps/web/e2e/stage-fit.spec.ts is what notices: it measures the page against the stage, which no golden shot can do because the crop is the SVG element and the defect is the space around it. Note which box a new handler measures its origin against — `view.x/y` are *layer*-relative, and reading a rect off the stage instead is the §7 ⑨ defect, invisible at rest because the anchor error is proportional to `(1 − zoom ratio)`. The last test in that file drives a real zoom and follows a point through the SVG's own user space, which is the only frame a transform does not move.

features.what: Show every ayah sharing an Arabic root with this one — the other way ayahs rhyme.

entry.note: Two shard families: per-ayah refs and per-root buckets. The split is what keeps a 44k-pair index inside the byte budget on a phone.
Ranking for someone holding a mushaf: near pages first, because that is how the memory is organised.

Which roots a word run actually carries — the word-granular half word-D added, and the seam between the two lenses. Every per-ayah root ref now names the PRINT word indices it sits at (`w`), baked in by the ETL, so this is a filter and not a second alignment. `Adjacency` has no root shards, so this is what a caller hands it as `options.roots` before asking `hopsForWords`; skip it and every shared-root edge is reported as unplaced rather than matched.
The ⬡ surface. Note the glyph is shared with a rail chip and the two promise different things — that collision was a decided defect, not an accident.

extend: Roots are derived, never hand-edited: change packages/etl/scripts/build-roots.mjs and re-run `make etl`.

Granularity is ayah-level in the UI and word-level in the data since word-D: each per-ayah ref carries `w`, the print word indices the root occupies, which is what `rootsForWords` reads. The ⬡ surface has not been narrowed to a run yet — that is a UI question, no longer a data one.

The `w` indices are the PRINT's, not the Quranic Arabic Corpus's, even though the roots themselves come from QAC. The ETL applies the alignment and ships the answer; nothing in L1 or L2 knows a second index exists, and re-introducing one here would undo placement C — see `word-indexing`.

features.what: Every view has a URL, and every URL restores its view — offline, from a cold start.

entry.note: State → hash. Its inverse `parseHash` must round-trip it; that pair is the whole contract and it is unit-tested as a pair.
Hash → state, and the place to be forgiving: a hand-typed or truncated link should degrade to something sensible rather than a blank page.
The React binding. Hash routing, not history routing, because this ships as static files with no server to rewrite paths.
Where a link leaves the app. Do not reach for the Clipboard API without a fallback — a LAN preview is plain http, so it is not a secure context and the API is simply absent.

The one query key that does not describe the view, and the only one that falls back instead of refusing a bad value. This list is the source of truth for the CSS blocks, the contrast rows and the catalog table.
The DOM half. Called from main.tsx before React mounts, because applying a field from an effect paints the default desk for one frame first — a white flash on `?field=dark`.

Binds parseHash, serializeState and docs/query-params.md to each other. It reads the failure-mode column against the code: a branch that can `return null` rejects, one that cannot falls back. It also binds tokens.css to DEFAULT_FIELD, because the document is painted before field.css is parsed and a drift there would show on exactly one frame.

extend: Add the key to `AppState`, then to both serializeState and parseHash in the same commit — a round-trip test is the cheapest way to keep them honest.

Decide, in writing, whether a bad value refuses the whole link or falls back to a default. Reject is the rule; falling back needs the argument `field` makes, which is that the key does not describe the view.
Add its row to docs/query-params.md, failure mode included — `gate:params` fails on a key with no row, and on a row that disagrees with the code.
Old links must keep working. Treat the hash format as a published API, because it is: it is in people's notes and messages.
Add an e2e that opens the URL cold, rather than one that clicks its way to the state — those test different things and only the first tests a link.

features.what: Getting to a known place: the surah/ayah jumper, the page bar along the bottom, the keyboard map, and the coach marks that teach the gestures once.

entry.note: Parses what someone actually types — Arabic or Western digits, Arabic names with or without alif-lam, '2:255', 'p19'. `normalizeArabic` is the reason it tolerates real input.
The combobox, opened from the one glyph in the header that is not a mode. The row it lives in has 17 px of slack on a 320 px phone — see chrome-fit before adding anything to it.

The header fits every phone from 320 to 430, and is the same height at all of them. The second half is the one that bites: the stage gets what the chrome leaves, and the golden baselines are shots of the stage.

The seam between the book's length and this build's inventory. The track spans the print (EditionMeta.pages — 604, and absent for editions nobody has counted); the landing is whatever is in public/assets. `nearestPage` answers with what it *did*, so the caller can say so.

The bottom bar: a 604-long track with a page turn on each edge, pinned RTL in both languages so page 1 sits on the right. Two traps live here — it commits on the native `change` event, not React's `onChange` (which is `input`, and would mount a 170 KB SVG per value crossed), and it takes the arrow keys itself, because a range's own step of 1-of-604 snaps straight back inside a three-page inventory.
One pure function from (key, context) to action, so the keyboard map is testable without a DOM and cannot disagree with itself across components.
Shown once, keyed in localStorage. Every e2e that is not about coach marks must suppress them in an init script, or it is testing the coach marks.

extend: New input syntax: extend parseJump and its unit tests. Keep the UI dumb — it should render JumpTargets, not know how they were found.
New shortcut: add it to appKeyAction with a KeyContext branch, and add the row to the help surface in the same commit.
Anything added to the header row costs width the row does not have, and height the stage cannot spare. Run chrome-fit before and after, and if it needs a control, say which one it replaces.

Vendoring pages: the page bar's *copy* needed no change when Loop 4b filled the print — the track was already the whole print, so it went from «٣ من ٦٠٤» to «٦٠٤ من ٦٠٤» on its own. `pagesVendored` stays: it is not a caveat that expires, it is the bar saying what is behind it, and the next edition may carry half a mus'haf. Its *picture* did need a change and did not get one for a loop: the inventory was drawn one span per vendored page, which was three marks at three pages and 604 overlapping ones at 604 — a solid rail saying nothing, reconciled on every value a dragged thumb passed over. It is drawn as `pageRuns` now, one node per contiguous stretch, so the cost follows the number of gaps rather than the length of the book. The lesson generalises past this bar: a picture whose node count is the size of the corpus is a picture that was only ever tested on a small corpus. The snap is the other thing to watch — it used to fire on nearly every drag and now fires almost never, so e2e/pagebar.spec.ts trims a page out of the manifest to keep testing the branch rather than testing that it never runs.

The page bar is the bottom-most chrome, so it owns the home-indicator inset. If anything is ever put below it, the inset moves with it — two elements padding for it is a doubled gap, neither is a control under the indicator.

features.what: Which mushaf print you are reading, and whether tajweed colouring is on.

entry.note: The registry. `EditionStatus` is what keeps an edition whose provenance is still PROVISIONAL out of the picker.
Maps an ayah between editions. Needed because ayah numbering is not universal and a share link must survive an edition switch.

Per-surah mark shards → per-ayah marks. `TAJWEED_RULES` is the seven-colour PAINTING vocabulary — not the source's, which has eighteen entries and lives in data. Two vocabularies rather than one is the whole shape of this feature: a shard says `ikhfa_shafawi`, `rules.json` says that paints as `ghunnah`, and `marksForAyah` folds the two at read time. Core is deliberately ignorant of which source it is reading, so it validates the mapping (`parseTajweedVocabulary`) instead of hard-coding it, and paints NOTHING until the mapping lands — a shard on its own is offsets keyed by strings this layer has never been taught.

Where the eighteen become seven. It folds every source rule sharing a family into one mark, keeps both source names on `TajweedMark.sources`, and orders the result by `TAJWEED_RULES` so the rarest rule still wins the ayah. The fold used to happen in the build, which is why nothing downstream could tell an ikhfa from an iqlab; moving it here cost +17.5% gzipped on the shards and is what makes a finer legend — or a reader-editable palette — possible at all.

The eighteen-to-seven table, and the only place it exists. It stays in L3 because it is a fact about *this source's* vocabulary rather than about tajweed: a different corpus with a different rule list would need a different table and no core code would change. The build writes it out as `tajweed/rules.json` beside the shards, so the mapping ships as data a reader can inspect rather than as a decision baked into 114 files.
The switch. Skin swap must not re-render the stage — it changes classes on existing nodes.

The gate the two-vocabulary shape made necessary. A shard key with no entry in `rules.json` paints NOTHING — no error, no blank page, no console warning, because painting an unplaceable rule some default colour would be worse. The symptom is a rule that quietly stops appearing on every page, and the only witness is a hafiz who noticed the ghunnah went silent. It reads the SHIPPED bytes rather than the build's table, on purpose: whether the table is right is not the question, whether the 114 files a browser will fetch agree with the file beside them is. Both directions — an id no vocabulary describes, and a vocabulary entry no shard uses — plus the two ends it is bolted to: a family core does not paint, and a family with no colour or dash pattern in tokens.css.

extend: A new edition is a data change first: assets, a SOURCES.md entry with its licence, and a concordance. Only then a registry entry.
gate:license and gate:text-sources both read SOURCES.md — an edition whose provenance is not recorded cannot ship, by construction.

A new PAINTED family: add to TAJWEED_RULES, add the palette entry, add its label to both message catalogues. The class prefix is centralised so CSS and TS cannot drift. Seven is not arbitrary — it is the most a colour-blind-safe qualitative palette carries honestly on cream paper, so an eighth is a palette decision before it is a code change.

A new SOURCE rule is not that. It goes in build-tajweed.mjs's table pointing at a family that already exists; the build throws on an id the table does not name, so a source refresh that adds one fails loudly instead of dropping it.

features.what: Which language the chrome speaks — and the much longer list of things that never change with it.

entry.note: What a locale has to declare before it can render anything: its name in itself, the abbreviation of that name the desktop header's switch wears, its chrome direction, its surah-name table, its digits, and which spelling of a tajweed rule it puts first. Keyed by a `Lang` derived from the catalogs, so dropping in messages/ur.json fails to compile until Urdu has answered all six. None of them has a defensible default — a locale silently inheriting `ltr` is a mus'haf rendered backwards, and nothing shortens «العربية» to «ع» by rule, which is why `abbr` is declared here rather than truncated at the call site.

The opening language: a stored choice, then the device, then Arabic. React-free and CSS-free on purpose — main.tsx calls it before mount so the document's lang/dir are right on the first paint, and e2e/lang.spec.ts imports LANG_STORAGE_KEY from here rather than retyping it.

The reason this is a framework and not a table. Arabic has six CLDR plural categories and `few` is n % 100 = 3..10, not n <= 10 — which is what the hand-written ternary said, wrongly, for 41 of the 603 distances the mus'haf can produce. ICU MessageFormat states the six forms; Intl.PluralRules picks between them. Compiled at build time by scripts/messages-compile.mjs; the parser is a devDependency and ships zero bytes.

The shape every component reads, unchanged by the migration to compiled catalogs so that no call site moved. It is no longer where completeness is enforced — that is one layer down, in `const messages: Catalog` inside each messages/*.gen.ts, which is stricter because it checks argument names and not just arity. There is still no runtime lookup that can miss and no fallback chain.

The assembler: one function, run for every locale, wiring a compiled catalog to format.ts's formatters and to LOCALES. Written once is the point — the old file said everything twice, so «صفحتان» and "2 pages" were two independent chances to bind a rule differently. It also holds the numeral convention: {n} selects a plural form, {nText} is digits(n, lang) and is what prints, and a bare {page} is a raw number, i.e. Latin digits in every language.

Binds the chosen bundle, the formatters and `dir` into one context. Mounted in main.tsx, not App: the default context is Arabic with an inert setter, so every component test written before this feature renders bare and still reads Arabic.

The four holes tsc cannot see: generated code left stale after a catalog edit, a key the reference locale has and a translation does not, a plural that writes four of Arabic's six categories, and a translation that drops a placeholder. Plural completeness is checked against Intl.PluralRules(locale) — the same CLDR the runtime will use, not a table in this repo. Registered in package.json, the Makefile and ci.yml; a gate in one of the three does not run.

Names and numerals are presentation, so they live here and not in core — `parseJump` takes the table as an argument, the same injection `enhancePolygons` uses for labelFor. Every function in this file takes an explicit `lang` and none defaults it.

entry.symbol: the mus'haf, the rail, the trail and the page bar stay right-to-left
entry.note: The assertion that matters most, and the one unit tests cannot reach: with an English chrome, `main` and `footer` still compute `direction: rtl`. The stylesheet is 100% logical properties, which is what makes the flip a one-line change and also what makes an accidental inherited flip move the hop rail to the wrong thumb.

extend: New user-facing copy is a key in every messages/*.json, then `pnpm i18n:build`, then a line in buildStrings. Never a literal in a component — the compiler is what stops an English build shipping an Arabic sentence, and a key missing from one locale does not compile.

Anything that counts takes two arguments: {n} for the plural to select on and {nText} for the digits that print. The emitter rejects ICU's `#` and {n, number} on purpose — they route through Intl.NumberFormat, which is a second numeral authority and disagrees with format.ts's digits().

Adding a language is a JSON catalog plus a LOCALES row; there is no union to widen and no import to add, because Lang and CATALOGS are derived from the files in messages/. The full checklist is docs/design/i18n.md §⑦.

Both language switches — Colophon's and DesktopChrome's — map LOCALE_IDS over LOCALES, so a third locale grows a third option with no edit. Do not reintroduce anything shaped like `other`: a field meaning "the language this one is not" is well defined at two locales and silently wrong at three, where it renders one option short and puts the same name on two buttons. The tests are written over LOCALE_IDS for that reason and will name the language the switch left out.

Ask whether the new text is chrome or scripture. Chrome translates and follows `dir`; anything quoting the mus'haf, a verse, a root, or a licence credit pins `lang="ar" dir="rtl"` and is translated by nobody.
i18n.test.tsx walks LOCALE_IDS and calls every formatter, so a new key is covered the day it exists and a new locale the day its catalog lands.

The e2e suite is pinned to `locale: "ar"` in playwright.config.ts because that is what every aria snapshot and golden image was recorded in. lang.spec.ts is the one file that overrides it, and a second such file should say why.

features.what: On a wide screen the app shows an open mus'haf — two leaves and a spine — and says plainly which half it does not have.

entry.symbol: Hifth is a navigation instrument for huffaz
entry.note: Read this before touching anything below. It carries the arithmetic behind the breakpoint, the governing rule for what desktop is allowed to add, and §4's table of what changed when the print was vendored. docs/decisions/desktop-vs-mobile.md is the running table of individual decisions; append a row there rather than restating one here.

Which two pages face each other. The mus'haf reads right to left, so the *lower* number is the right-hand leaf, and the print pairs (1,2), (3,4)… — odd on the right, which is why Al-Fatiha faces Al-Baqarah and why 604 pages make 302 openings with no orphan. This is pagination, not presentation, which is why it sits in core beside nearestPage and why no component re-derives it; its doc comment records where the parity was observed and why the phase it used to implement was wrong.

The one breakpoint, and the only copy of record. Two axes because a mus'haf leaf is portrait: leaf width comes from the height the chrome leaves, so a width-only query would hand a 1440x700 window less page than a 320px phone. Repeated as a literal in DesktopChrome.module.css only because CSS cannot read a custom property inside a media query; useMediaQuery.test.ts reads that stylesheet back so the two cannot drift.

The two leaves. Sides are declared exactly once — right leaf first in DOM order, inside main[dir="rtl"] — so there is no row-reverse or `order` that could disagree with appKeyAction's ArrowLeft = +1. `enabled` gates the *mount*, not the styling: a display:none leaf still fetches its ~170 KB SVG and builds a Highlighter. Three boxes, and the two testids are how tests tell them apart: .spread (page-spread) is the desk and runs the window's width, .book (page-book) is the two leaves and nothing else — it carries the gutter, clips the parked band, and is what the fold portals into — and .leaf is one page, sized block-size:100% + aspect-ratio 345/550 rather than flex: 1 1 0.

One of three knobs (with --stage-field and --stage-pad) that are the whole coupling between the spread's stylesheet and the stage's. CSS modules hash their class names, so a custom property is the only way one can size the other; every fallback is the phone's own behaviour, so PageStage needed no change at all. In a spread all three are neutralised — cap 100%, field none, pad 0 — because the leaf is already exactly a page and the desk already painted the field.

The controls a phone had no room for (the language switch, two levels deep in the colophon sheet because chrome-fit holds the header inside 320px with 17px of slack) and no use for (the keyboard map), plus the two that exist because a desktop has a second leaf to close: the page-mode radiogroup and the zoom stepper. Hidden by CSS rather than unmounted, unlike the spread — these are spans and buttons, not a second mus'haf. The chrome decides nothing: it renders `pageMode`/`zoom` and calls back. The stepper is disabled while the book is open and says why on the control itself, which is the ordering that replaced a derivation — see ZOOM_STEPS.

The nine rungs the stepper climbs, exported because the chrome needs to know where the ends are — a disabled button at the floor is the ladder being stated rather than discovered by clicking. A ladder and not a multiplier because a button is pressed a countable number of times and should land on a nameable level; the spacing keeps the old wheel ratio's feel, and `rung(z, step)` takes the nearest rung STRICTLY past z, because zoom also arrives from a hop at DEFAULT_HOP_ZOOM 1.55, which is not on the ladder. Every zoom on this stage goes through zoomAbout, and setZoom anchors at the LAYER centre — never the stage, never the host. Do not write a second copy of that arithmetic; pass an origin. docs/decisions/wheel-and-zoom.md.

Thirty entries, the first page of each juz, or null for a juz this build does not carry. Built on juzOfPage rather than on a second membership rule — the repo forbids a second copy of that. Memoised once at the App level because its caller is a wheel: shift+wheel is an array index, not a 604-page scan. A juz boundary page belongs to two juz at once and this deliberately disagrees with juzOfPage about page 22 — juzOfPage calls it juz 1's, this calls it juz 2's START, and both are true of the same sheet.

entry.symbol: ctrl+wheel does nothing at all — it is somebody else's pinch
entry.note: The assertion that a binding is absent, which is the only kind that rots silently. On macOS a trackpad pinch arrives as ctrl+wheel with the modifier synthesised by the OS, so anything bound here fires on a pinch — bound to juz it teleports ~20 pages, left unbound it hands the window to browser page zoom, which changes what a CSS pixel is and bounces DESKTOP_QUERY. So it is preventDefaulted and dropped, and this row is what stops someone reclaiming it. The jump lives on shift+wheel, which reads deltaY || deltaX because several browsers deliver a shifted wheel horizontally.

entry.symbol: puts the lower page number on the right
entry.note: The assertion the unit tests cannot make. They check DOM order; DOM order only becomes *sides* once an RTL flow has run, so a flex-direction: row-reverse added by someone 'fixing' the layout passes all nine component tests and puts the mus'haf on backwards. Verified by inducing exactly that.

extend: Before adding anything to the desktop layout, name the mobile constraint that put it out of reach. If you cannot, it is a new feature and belongs in the PLAN, not in a media query — that is the governing rule in docs/design/desktop.md §1.

A new desktop decision is a row appended to docs/decisions/desktop-vs-mobile.md: what mobile does, what desktop does, and why they differ. The design doc links to that table rather than duplicating it.

Loop 4b vendored the print, so `renderFacing` is no longer fixture-only — every spread is two real leaves, and the honest hole is now reached by trimming a page out of the manifest (apps/web/e2e/inventory.ts). Nothing about the geometry changed; see docs/design/desktop.md §4 for the table of what did.

The wheel navigates and buttons magnify. Do not derive page mode from zoom, or zoom from anything: that was built, and one state with two owners leaked three ways (the facing leaf zoomed alone; a breakpoint crossing kept the mode and lost the view; the range below fit read as 'at fit'). pageMode and zoom are explicit state in App, written in one place, and the chrome only asks. docs/decisions/wheel-and-zoom.md.

entry.note: Registration and update flow. Service workers need a secure context — that is why offline specs cannot pass against a plain-http LAN or container URL, and it is the harness, not the app.

Eviction takes the precache and leaves the registration, so the worker never installs again and offline dies silently while every online signal still says healthy. The repair re-registers the same sw.js under a query-suffixed URL, because only a script the registration has never seen produces an install — measured, not assumed: reloads, update(), and unregister()+register() all leave the precache empty or resurrect the old worker. It waits for that install to finish, not for index.html to reappear: the shell is the first entry written and the app's scripts are the last.
Asks the browser not to evict us. It can say no, and the honest UI for that is a notice, not silence.

What the user is told about their storage — and the only place the install prompt is offered. Must not stack with the coach strip; must not move into the header, which has no width for it. Loop 6b gave it a third thing to say: a pinned juz that a sweep took, which is the one storage message that arrives with a repair rather than a warning.

Loop 6b: which files a pinned juz is made of. Read off the manifest's pages, never off JUZ_STARTS — the table says where a juz begins, the manifest says which paper exists, and a plan built from the first would promise pages the build has no SVG for. It counts those absent ayahs instead of hiding them, which is why the offer can say so before the reader spends the bytes.

A pack lives in its own Cache Storage bucket with no expiration plugin, and assets.ts reads it before the network. Warming the service worker's hifth-pages instead would have been simpler and is wrong: that cache is a 32-entry LRU sized for a browsing trail, so pinning a juz and then reading twelve pages evicts a third of what was pinned, and nobody finds out until the plane. Bytes in Cache Storage, the claim in IndexedDB — the split is what makes a sweep detectable rather than merely silent.

The one thing a pin tells the service worker: this fetch is not a read for display. Both runtimeCaching routes in vite.config.ts decline anything carrying it, so a pinned file is written once instead of also landing in hifth-pages and evicting the trail it was meant to preserve (backlog ⑮). The literal is deliberately duplicated into vite.config.ts and must stay in step: workbox generateSW stringifies a route matcher, so an imported constant reaches the worker as undefined and the route silently declines nothing. Static provenance is the whole contract — the worker never learns PACK_CACHE's name, the pack's URL list, or that a register exists, so planPack can change shape without sw.js moving. See docs/decisions/pin-marker.md.

The pin control and the shelf of what is kept, inside the revision map at juz scope — the map is already the picture of the thirty, and the header has no room for a sixth button. The states are named in words, in a list, not painted as a dot on a cell: the cells already carry warmth and absence, and the meaning that would be misread is exactly the one that matters, a swept pack looking pinned.

Pinning writes every file twice — pinPack fetches through the page, so the service worker's CacheFirst route caches the same bytes — which means an offline test can pass with the pack deleted. Deleting the outside copy is not a workaround: it is the state a pinned juz is genuinely in once ordinary reading pushes it out of that LRU, and the only state in which the assertion means what it says.

extend: Precache list and strategies live in the vite-plugin-pwa config in apps/web/vite.config.ts, not in a hand-written sw.js.
Adding to the precache costs install-time bytes on a phone. Check the entry count and size the build prints.
Test offline behaviour in an e2e that actually goes offline, over a secure context. A unit test cannot see a service worker.

Eviction is a separate case from offline and has its own describe in apps/web/e2e/offline.spec.ts: CDP Storage.clearDataForOrigin with storageTypes 'cache_storage' takes the caches and leaves the worker registered, which is the state a real ITP sweep leaves behind.

Anything the reader chose to keep does not go in a runtime cache. It goes in the pack cache, and something has to be able to notice it is gone — a store with no register against it can only ever report success.

A new runtimeCaching route needs the !request.headers.has("X-Hifth-Pin") clause too, or pinning starts filing duplicates in it. From a controlled page there is no fetch the worker cannot see — cache.add is routed the same way, measured — so a pin is recognised and declined rather than hidden. What the worker may know about a pack stops at that one bit; anything about the pack's shape belongs in packs.ts.
Anything that can fail to load a page must say so — see PageStage's error banner. A silent failure leaves the previous page on the stage while the chrome has already announced the new number.

features.what: The mushaf SVG pages themselves, and the polygon metadata that makes them clickable.

entry.note: Source SVG → the page asset plus its polygon manifest. Deterministic by requirement: CI re-runs it and fails on any byte of difference.
Fetch and cache a page in the browser. The one place that knows the asset URL shape.

The ceiling on how many page SVGs stay in the DOM (backlog ③), and the reason vendoring 604 pages did not turn a long reading session into a leak: `MOUNTED_PAGE_CAP` mounted nodes, evicted least-recently-used, with the pages a turn is animating between pinned so the leaf being turned cannot be collected mid-flight. A spread mounts two leaves at once, so `spreadBudget` splits the same cap rather than doubling it — App.tsx passes each stage its share.

Loop 4b: the whole print, fetched from the pinned upstream, optimised the way Loop 0 optimised its three, and written unpadded (`8.svg`, not `008.svg`). It reproduces pages 7, 9 and 19 byte for byte before it will vendor anything else — a run that cannot rebuild what is already committed has changed the pipeline, not extended the corpus. Three transforms stand between upstream and what ships, all declared in the header and all asserted by exact count: svgo at the pinned version and config, `ID_REPAIRS` (two polygons whose `id` holds path geometry), and `POLYGON_REPAIRS` (PLAN 14 — 21 tap targets that did not cover their own ayah). The last runs *before* svgo, because svgo rewrites path data at `floatPrecision 1` and a repair written against optimised output would be matching our own rounding rather than upstream's bytes.

The wire form the app fetches. 604 pages of per-ayah polygons is megabytes; the compact form is one 6236-long array indexed by absolute ayah, 1.3 KB gzipped, so the manifest stayed a single eager request instead of becoming a shard. A page an edition lacks is written as `0` and skipped on expand — that zero is what every honest-hole path downstream is reading.

Cross-checks the vendored pages against the QUL V2 pin: the count, the filename shape, and the anchor ayahs on sampled pages. `audit-corpus` asks whether the manifest covers the print; this asks whether the paper under it is the print we pinned. Since PLAN 14 it also asks the one question every identity check misses — is every glyph of scripture inside a box a finger can reach — and it asks it by measurement, not by signature: map the ink through the page matrix and test each glyph's centre against the polygons. The two signatures that preceded it pattern-matched shapes already known and missed seven pages, four of them because the rule excused any page whose first polygon is an `X:1`. What replaced them is `ORPHAN` (a glyph outside every polygon and every furniture band) and `BAND` (a furniture band taller than two line-heights, so it has swallowed scripture), both demanding zero — possible only because the 12-unit tolerance was measured (benign glyphs stray 8.8 units, defects a median 36) rather than chosen. Furniture is inferred, never listed: it is a gap in the polygon tiling that a surah's first ayah picks up directly below. There is deliberately no allow-list — this gate knows nothing of `vendor-pages.mjs`'s repair table, so a regressed repair and a newly-broken upstream fail alike.
Does the corpus actually cover what we claim? Coverage assumed rather than measured is how a missing page reaches a memoriser.

What the corpus weighs, and the ceilings. pages/ is gated per page plus a 604-page projection rather than by a total, because a total ceiling on the one kind that grows would have to be raised by the very change it exists to watch.

Asks of a corpus we have not adopted the one question adoption turns on: which print does it paginate? Reads the candidate's own `data-surah`/`data-aya` and compares each page's ayah span against `ayah-pages.json` — no fonts, no rendering, no judgment. The page set is every V1/V2 divergence band plus controls outside them, because contested pages alone cannot separate "this corpus is V2" from "our table is wrong in exactly the contested places". Named `probe-` and not `gate-`: it reaches the public internet and answers a question, and its answer lives in `ligature-svg.probe.json` beside the fetched pages' hashes.

The second question about the same unadopted corpus, and the one word-level selection was blocked on: do their word boxes land on our paper? Fits a 4-parameter axis-aligned affine per page from the one landmark both corpora carry independently — the ayah-end ornament — and then checks every word centre falls inside the ayah polygon its own attributes name. The answer (`word-registration.probe.json`) is that scale is 1.3333 both axes and the offsets are the two constants already sitting in our own SVGs' transform matrices, one per page parity; residual is sub-pixel, so the per-page fit is a check rather than a necessity. Reuses `ligature-svg.probe.json`'s pin — one pin, not two — so a corpus that moves invalidates both probes at once.

extend: Never hand-edit anything under apps/web/public/assets — it is generated, and the ETL determinism check in CI will reject it.

A corpus considered and not adopted still leaves evidence: probe it against a pinned commit, hash what you fetched, and commit the verdict (`ligature-svg.probe.json`). A decision remembered instead of recorded gets re-litigated by the next loop that wants word geometry.

Two coordinate spaces live in one page SVG: the ink sits under `matrix(1.3333 0 0 -1.3333 -115|-55 640)` and is y-flipped, the ayah polygons sit outside it in plain top-down viewBox space. Anything mapping external geometry onto a polygon works in the second space and must not apply the matrix — `probe-word-registration.mjs`'s header records how that was established.
Change the producing script, run `make etl`, and commit the script and the regenerated output together.
gate:notext enforces that pages carry no <text> nodes: the glyphs are outlines, so rendering never depends on a font being installed.

A new kind of asset needs a ceiling in gate-assets.mjs CEILINGS before it can land — the gate fails on a directory it does not recognise, on purpose, because silently skipping the unfamiliar is the defect it closes.

features.what: A rectangle per word on the mushaf page — measured off a second print of the same mus'haf and moved onto ours.

entry.note: The one copy of the arithmetic that puts two prints of the same page into one coordinate system. Both corpora mark the end of every ayah with an ornament, so the ornaments are a correspondence neither was built to provide: `readTheirs`/`readOurs` pull them out, `readingOrder` puts both lists in the same order (line bands right-to-left, which is the only ordering an RTL page can be paired in), and `fit` solves `ours = s·theirs + t` per axis by least squares. Everything else here is the plumbing that has to be exact for that to mean anything — `pathBBox` with real cubic extrema rather than control-point hulls, `ringsOf`/`pointInRings` for testing a point against a multi-subpath polygon. It is a library and not a script because three callers need identical answers; two copies of a least-squares fit that disagree in the sixth decimal are two different mus'hafs. **What it fits on is not what it is used for, and that gap is the largest measured error in the pipeline.** The ornaments are the only correspondence the two corpora both label, so they are the fiducials; the marks and word boxes this fit then places are the target, and the fit's own residual grades itself excellent while being a full mark-height wrong — page 7 closes to 0.0912 units and its ink is out by about 1.0. Across 604 pages the residual correlates **0.117** with the real error, and read per component it is worse than uninformative: **0.019** against the irreducible per-page scatter and **−0.022** against `|dty|`, the largest term, while managing 0.302 against `|dtx|`, so it grades hardest on the part that matters least. That is Fitzpatrick's fiducial-vs-target result reproduced in a mus'haf, and it is why three sessions of arguing about this residual moved a number and not the problem — the reasons, the citations and the remedy are in `docs/design/mark-registration.md`. Nothing here is wrong; the caution is about what its output may be asked to do. Correcting it is the open decision `mark-placement`.

One fetch of the upstream corpus, cached on disk under `data/pages/.cache/words`, hashed on the way in and checked against `ligature-svg.probe.json`'s pin on the way out. 378 MB is read to produce 2.2 MB, and it is read by a probe and a builder that must see the same bytes — so `{ offline: true }` is a real mode, not a convenience: it refuses to reach the network and fails if the cache is cold, which is how a determinism re-run proves it re-derived rather than re-downloaded.

The builder: 604 shards of word boxes on our viewBox, plus `word-boxes.pin.json` (a SHA-256 per upstream page and per shard). Per page it fits the frame, transfers every `<g id="md-word-…">`'s bbox through it, and asserts the fit's residual is under a ceiling — 2.0 units on the standard frame, 3.0 on the two override pages, both measured against an observed max of 2.722 rather than picked. Pause marks are separated from lexical words (`isPauseMark`) because they are the only boxes that legitimately sit outside their ayah's polygon, hanging below the line. A page whose ornaments cannot be paired borrows its parity group's median transform rather than guessing, and says which pages borrowed.

Re-measures every committed box against the polygon it claims — offline, and with its own path parser rather than the ETL's, because a gate that imports the code it is checking only proves the code agrees with itself. Three checks: LEXICAL (a word's centre is inside its own ayah), MARK (a pause mark's bottom edge meets its polygon within `MARK_DROP`, 4 units — measured: 4,453 of 4,486 need nothing and the worst needs 2.9), PAIRING (shard keys and polygon keys match in both directions, 604 pages, zero either way). This is the gate that found the one defect `gate:pages` structurally cannot see: on p577 the ink of 75:5's first word *was* covered by a tappable box — the wrong ayah's. No orphan, so no orphan check could fire. Two prints of the same page can say that; one cannot.

entry.symbol: The blocker was never that the marks are anonymous
entry.note: The design of record for the level below a word, and the answer to "can Hifth highlight the tanween?". Read it before touching `skins.ts`'s ayah-granularity comment, which it demotes from a design constraint to a stale sentence (§⑧ ③). Also the place §② keeps two different things called a mark apart: the word shards' `marks` are *pause* marks and their integers are word indices, while these are drawn inside a word — which is why the asset kind would be `diacritics` and why `DIACRITICS` deliberately cannot name a waqf sign.

The level below a word: the twenty-six names the ligature corpus draws above and below a letter, in the order an id means. A shard says `0`, not `"fatha"`, because a page carries ~540 marks and the names are the larger half of the bytes — which makes the array's *order* load-bearing in a way nothing else here is. Appending is safe; reordering silently re-labels the whole corpus and changes no geometry, so nothing downstream would notice. `diacritics.test.ts` pins six ids for that reason. Deliberately excludes the dots (`data-dots`, 105,269 paths, three values): i'jam is part of the letter's identity, not a mark a reader is told to look at. It lives in core and not in the ETL because it is the one place the vocabulary is written down — `build-tajweed.mjs`'s arrangement with `isTajweedRuleId`, for the same reason.

A named, exact box per mark, on our frame, grouped by the word it sits on. Fits nothing: `apply` is handed in, rebuilt by `applierFromPin` from the four numbers `word-boxes.pin.json` already records, so a mark cannot end up on a second transform that disagrees with its own word's by a tenth of a unit. The invariant that makes this verifiable offline is that a word's shipped box is the union over *every* path in its segment, marks included — so containment holds by construction, and an escape can only be an alignment error, a mark filed under the wrong word. Throws on a `data-diacritic` core has never heard of rather than inventing an id, and its `attr` docblock records the regex trap that cost a corpus-wide run of `[Infinity, …, -Infinity]` boxes: the leading `\s` is load-bearing, because `d` otherwise matches the tail of `id="md-path-…"`. **The four numbers it is handed are page-global, and a page is measurably the wrong grain for a mark.** `applierFromPin` rebuilds one scale and one translation for the whole page, which is the right shape for a word box 22 units wide and too coarse for a mark 5.6 by 3.6: after the best per-page correction, 19.49% of marks still land further than 0.75 units from their own ink, and adding a scale term to that page-global family buys 1.8% of the across-scatter and makes 189 of 600 pages worse — the four-number family is exhausted, not under-fitted. The grain that survives arithmetic is the **printed line**: ~15 groups a page at ~36 marks each, above the floor a median needs, where word is ~3.75 marks a group and would fit noise, and per-mark is excluded on purpose because letting each rectangle snap to its own nearest ink is how "it is drawn on the wrong mark" gets manufactured. The line is also the physically motivated unit — justification is set per line, so two prints that set a line differently slide every word on it together — and it is nearly free here, because `<g id="md-word-NNN">` already carries `data-line-number` and only that one field has to be carried through. What to actually do about it is the open decision `mark-placement`, and the fork this function sits on is its option G: whether a finer correction moves the marks alone or the word boxes with them.

The measurement that had to come before anything shipped, over all 604 cached pages: the vocabulary is complete (26 of 26 names drawn), every one of 326,515 marks lands inside the word box the app already ships (0 escapes, 0 unmatched, slack 0.2 — rounding, not registration), and the shard tree would weigh 7.35 MB raw / 2.28 MB gz. Containment is checked against the *committed* shards rather than boxes computed in the same pass, so the two sides cannot share a mistake and agree about it. It ships nothing on purpose: 2.28 MB of assets no caller fetches is the same waste `gate:assets` names for a non-vendored edition. Five questions, and the order between them is the argument: ④ establishes that the counts work out per ligature, and only then does ⑤ establish which path is which. What none of them can answer is whether the ink lands where a reader's eye goes — that needs an eye, and belongs in the encoding inspector.

⑤'s engine, and the reason the codepoint→name dictionary is evidence rather than an assumption. Arc consistency over bipartite matchings: a run contributes a *bag* of codepoint tokens beside a *bag* of drawn names, and a pairing is deleted only when no perfect one-to-one assignment of that run can use it. Position is never consulted — pairing them off left to right would assume the print draws marks in written order, which is the thing in question, and 1.36% of multi-mark runs say otherwise. Plain set intersection is the wrong operator and was tried first: it presumes the relation is already a function, and drove `U+0653` to an empty candidate set, which is how the `أ`-carrier madda convention was found. Every single-mark run is held out, because a one-mark run forces its own pairing and scoring against it would report 100% by construction. Result: 34 of 34 tokens pinned in two passes, 62,931 of 62,931 held-out runs predicted correctly.

④ and ⑤'s arithmetic extracted so there is exactly one of it, and the only entry point a caller should want: a word as `readDiacritics` returns it → `[{ at, len, token, name, mark }]`, where `at` is a **codepoint** index into that word's own `data-hafs`. That index is the whole point — tajweed offsets count codepoints, so this is the bridge from an offset to a rectangle. Three steps behind it: `letters` folds `\p{Mn}` *and* `\p{Lm}` onto the letter before (the tatweel and the small waw/yeh are text letters the print draws as marks, which is what made ④'s first draft off by one for every seated hamza), `align` matches ligatures to letter runs by CONTENT with backtracking (order is not reading order — «ٱلرَّحِيمِ» draws `[لر|حيم|ٱ]`, and a left-to-right walk agreed on every length while misassigning every mark), and `pairMarks` pairs a wanted token to a drawn name through the frozen 34-entry `DRAWN_NAME`, breaking same-name ties right to left. Its refusals are the load-bearing part: it returns `null` — never a partial answer — for a mark count that disagrees, a name the tokens did not ask for, or letters no assignment of ligatures can cover, because a partial answer would look exactly like an answer. Extracted rather than left in the probe for the reason `tajweed-fold.mjs` gives about itself: `probe-encodings.mjs --marks` draws these rectangles, and if its join were a second implementation, a clean screen would stop being evidence about the probe.

28 tests on words small enough to count by hand, and most of them assert that `markPaths` returns `null`. The probe is the measurement — 86,962 words joined, 34 tokens pinned — and it needs 380 MB of gitignored cache to say anything, which is why it is a probe; what a test can hold is the arithmetic and the refusals. Marks are written as `[diacriticId(name), x, y, w, h]` rather than pasted ids, so reordering `DIACRITICS` fails here instead of silently re-labelling what this file claims. One test earned its comment the hard way: `مَـَٔ` yields three tokens, not two — the tatweel and the sajda overline get no path, but the hamza-above on the tatweel does.

The mark-C decision drawn on the print instead of argued: three overlays over page 2 — what ships today, what mark granularity would paint, and geometry-only — so the choice is looked at rather than described. Its finding is the one the option cards exist to carry: at ayah granularity **50,023 of 60,057 annotations (83.29%) render as nothing**, because an ayah carries 3.90 distinct families on average and `leadingRule` paints exactly one; `madd` is annotated on 92.48% of ayahs and wins 2.74% of them. So the constraint the skin is under is not that a wash is coarse, it is that a wash is *singular*, and that is what finer selection buys. Split in two on purpose: `--extract` needs the 348 MB gitignored page cache and writes `mark-granularity.data.json`, while the default render reads only committed bytes, so any checkout reproduces the identical HTML without the cache — the same bargain `probe-diacritics.mjs` makes, one step further along. Every rectangle on it is traceable: word boxes from the shipped shard, mark boxes from `markPaths` through `applierFromPin`, ayah polygons from the page's own `verse-N` hit shapes, colours and dashes read out of `tokens.css` at build time so the picture cannot drift from the app. It references the print by relative URL rather than inlining it — 42 KB, not 256 KB, and no second copy of bytes the repo already ships. Its `attr` reader carries the same leading-`\s` boundary `diacritics.mjs` names, and for the same reason: without it `d` matches the tail of `id="verse-8"`, every ayah polygon gets `d="verse-8"`, and an unparseable `d` paints nothing and reports a zero bbox — so the "today" layer renders empty while the `<rect>`-based mark layer draws fine, which looks exactly like a wash being subtle.

Asks the question nothing before it asked: does a mark's rectangle sit on the ink a reader's eye goes to? Everything earlier counted ink INSIDE the box, which the base letter satisfies — so a box a full mark-height off scored as a hit. What makes this one different is the null control: every mark is also scored one width left, one width right, and on another mark's rectangle elsewhere on the page, and a claimed placement that cannot beat a deliberately wrong one is not a measurement. It does not. Over the full pass — 30,000 marks on all 604 pages, 2026-08-12 — separation is **−0.234** (claimed −0.120 against wrong +0.113), only **13.50%** of marks beat their own wrong placement, and the median rectangle overlaps the ink **0.017** against an achievable 0.909; the error is a shift of **0.81 across and 1.06 down** on marks 5.6 × 3.6, the same direction everywhere. Taking each page's own shift out is most of the repair and measurably not all of it: separation goes to **+0.281** and 75.7% of marks beat their null, but **19.49%** are still further than 0.75 units off and the corrected median overlap is 0.492 — so a single translation per page is a good model of this error, not a complete one, and whatever remains is not a page-level shift. The pipeline's recorded fit residual correlates 0.117 with the real error, which is why a number that looked like validation was blind to this. Exits non-zero on a breached threshold by design, and is deliberately NOT in `gates`, `make ci` or the Makefile — a probe reports, a gate refuses, and nothing should refuse until a person has worked the evidence page. Consumes the labelling verdict as its eligibility filter, so it is downstream of `probe-mark-labels.mjs` and not independent of it. **What `--shift-out` writes describes a SAMPLE of pages, and nothing downstream can tell.** `--sample` sets how many marks are drawn and `minMarksPerPage` throws away any page that got too few, so the emitted file holds a row per page that survived and no row at all for the rest — which is why it now writes a `coverage` block, ahead of the rows it qualifies. The default 4,000 marks at `--pages-n 40` reaches **40 pages of 604**; the full pass (`--pages-n 604 --sample 30000`, ~7 minutes) reaches **600 of 604**, the four missing being pages 1, 2, 603 and 604, whose ornamental frames never clear `minMarksPerPage`. Every by-eye trial needs a proposed move to start from, so both sessions so far could only be built on the original 40 — the correction is still validated exclusively on the pages it was fitted to, which is the open half of `the-correction-is-only-judged-where-it-was-fitted`. **The first 40 pages were representative in their mean and badly unrepresentative in their spread**: measuring the same 40 twice disagrees by about as much as those pages differ from each other, so the apparent variation there was mostly noise, and across all 604 the proposed moves span over 1.75 units rather than 0.31 — which is the leverage a placing session needs to measure the correction's size at all. Write a fuller pass to its own path (`mark-shift.604.json`), never over `mark-shift.json`: both scorers fingerprint the displacements and refuse a ruling made against different ones, so rewriting in place discards the answers of any session already worked. Both files are committed under `docs/validation/rulings/`, named with that fingerprint, so a banked verdict re-derives without rebuilding anything. A run at a finer grain adds a `perLine` block beside the per-page rows rather than replacing them — additive precisely so a page-grain run still writes the bytes it always wrote and every fingerprint already banked stays valid, and present at all because a grain that was measured and never written down is a finding rather than a correction. The per-page rows keep meaning exactly what they meant; the finer rows are read on top of them, and a line with no row falls back to its page.

Over what group are four numbers enough? Once a corpus-wide pass showed the per-page family exhausted — the best transform that could possibly be fitted to a page still leaves ~0.44 units of scatter across and ~0.34 down, and adding a scale term buys 1.8% of it while making 189 of 600 pages worse — the question stopped being *what are the four numbers* and became *what is the group*. A correction is a median or a least-squares fit over a group, so a grain is usable exactly when its groups still hold enough marks: page ~540, **line ~36** (p10 30 / p90 43, measured), word ~3.7, mark 1. The line is not a guess from our own numbers — two renderings of one text diverge because their glyph advances and line metrics differ, so error accumulates ALONG a line and resets at the next, which predicts a tilt within each line as well as an offset per line; `line-tilt` is that typographic prediction written down and it is the rung that wins. On 62,850 marks over 120 pages, fitted on half of each page and scored on the half it never saw, marks further than 0.75 units from their own ink go **17.5% (page) → 11.1% (line) → 4.5% (line tilt)**, against a shuffle null — every line wearing some other line's correction — at **31.2%**, which is far worse than no line correction at all and is what says the per-line numbers are facts rather than absorbed noise. Trained-on reads 3.1% against held-out 4.5%, so the gap is small and this is not overfitting. Nothing here rasterises: `dx, dy` already say where the ink is relative to the rectangle, so the residual under a candidate grain is arithmetic and a search over grains costs seconds — what it cannot say is how much ink a moved rectangle then COVERS, because overlap is not linear in displacement, and that only comes from re-scoring in `probe-mark-ink.mjs`. Extracted from that probe rather than left in it so the exploratory ladder and the shipped scorer run one implementation. Finer grains layer ON TOP of the page median, so a line too sparse to estimate falls back to its page rather than to nothing, and a page with no measured shift gets zero rather than a guess. **`SPLIT_FLOOR` is the trap this file names in its own docblock**: holding a split-half measurement to the production floor of 20 refuses a printed line that arrives at the fit with eighteen, so what gets measured is how many lines survived the halving rather than how well the grain works — at the production floor only 635 of 1,723 lines earned a correction and the grain read about three times weaker than it is. A floor sweep from 2 to 10 is completely flat, so the answer is not floor-sensitive.

entry.symbol: describe("a per-line correction, against a corpus that has per-line structure and one that does not"
entry.note: 25 tests on prints whose true difference we built ourselves, and the pair at the centre is the whole reason the file exists: two fixtures identical in page displacements, wobble and counts, differing only in whether their lines really move independently — and the flat one must **appear** to improve on the marks it was fitted to and then lose on the marks it never saw. A version of this file where both fixtures pass on trained-on numbers alone is a version that would have let us ship noise. Everything is deterministic (a seeded LCG, not `Math.random`) because a fixture that wobbles between runs cannot be argued from months later, which is the only reason these numbers exist. The floor suite reproduces the real trap at real scale: 36 marks a line, a quarter of them surviving the production floor after halving against 635 of 1,723 in the corpus. Three assertions were rewritten rather than loosened when they failed, and the reasons are in the file: a least-squares slope is not exactly orthogonal to an alternating residual over 40 points; a tilt fitted from 60 marks each carrying a quarter-unit of wobble is worth a tenth of a unit at the line's ends and not more; and `line-tilt` ties `line` on a flat corpus because a median offset and a least-squares intercept have comparable efficiency — so the honest claim is that tilt overfits harder and still loses to the PAGE grain, not that it loses to `line`.

The one measurement in this whole line of work that is not fitted to the thing it is graded by. Everything else moves a rectangle until it agrees with the ink and then reports how well it agrees with the ink, which improves with every parameter added — including when the parameter is fitting noise. The ayah-end ornaments are the escape: they are the only objects both corpora label, `word-boxes.pin.json`'s four numbers per page were fitted on them and nothing else, and the ink correction has never seen one. So it asks the inverse question — correct the text to sit on its ink, and where do the ornaments end up? Answer, over 1,305 pairs on 120 pages: **0.053 units under the shipped fit, 1.206 under the ink correction, worse on 120 of 120 pages**, and the same at every grain. The two printings genuinely agree about their ornaments and disagree about their text, so `mark-registration.md`'s old sentence "about the whole page" was too generous and now reads "about the whole page's text". The consequence for what ships is the reason this file exists rather than being a paragraph: the correction belongs to the words and the marks, and moving the ayah-end markers with it would break the one part of the page that is currently right. Pairs the ornaments with `readingOrder` exactly as `fitFrames` does, so these are the very points the shipped numbers were fitted on rather than a second opinion about which ornament is which; assigns each ornament a printed line from the word bands around it, because their ornaments carry no `data-line-number` and asking a per-line correction about the wrong line would make the test easier than it should be. Reads the rows a scoring run dumped (`probe-mark-ink.mjs --rows-out`) rather than fitting anything itself, takes seconds, writes nothing, and is a probe and not a gate for the usual reason.

The other half of the split, and the split is the point: whether a mark's rectangle is in the right PLACE and whether its NAME is right were once one number — "51.15%, or 69.15% counting look-alikes" — which was three unrelated effects added together. This half touches no shipped page, no fitted transform and no rectangle, so displacement cannot enter its arithmetic. A census over all 326,515 marks, so no confidence intervals: **256,948 (78.69%) match their own name · 69,562 (21.30%) match a name this print draws as the same shape · 5 anything else**, and those 5 have every stroke matching their own name at 0.83+, differing only in spacing. Genuine mislabels: zero. Three planted-label controls keep it honest — nearest wrong name flagged 100.00%, within-group 0.00%. Byte-identical across runs; exits 0.

A dependency-free SVG rasteriser, written rather than depended on for reasons that were measured, not assumed: two of the three npm rasterisers fetch a binary at install (so a determinism re-run cannot prove it re-derived), one drags an 18 MB text stack, and the pure-JS one implements neither fill rule correctly — on the same 5,600-sample shape nonzero says 6,400 and evenodd says 4,800. So both rules are honoured per-shape and OR-ed. Path flattening covers the full grammar including the arc form whose flags are written unseparated, which forces a character scanner rather than a number split. Summed-area tables make a rectangle's ink O(1), which is what lets a probe score 4,000 marks in three placements each.

The scorer, and the choice of scorer is load-bearing. Product-moment correlation of two binary masks (`phi`) DECIDES; Jaccard/IoU is reported and decides nothing, because IoU cannot go negative and so cannot tell 'wrong place' from 'nothing there' — the distinction the whole null control turns on. Two-stage search, quarter-unit coarse lattice then one-sample refine, ties broken toward the smaller displacement so a search cannot manufacture a better answer by moving further. Also `wilson`/`sampleSizeFor` for the intervals, `rng` (mulberry32, one stream per purpose so adding a control does not renumber the sample), and `chooseExemplars`, medoid-by-nearest-to-mean. An earlier version reported a correlation of 5.509 where the maximum is 1 — shared area and ink counted over different regions when a displacement pushed a shape off the raster edge — and it now throws rather than printing an impossible number.

One library of canonical examples, shared by both probes so they cannot drift into two vocabularies. `similarityMatrix` scores all 26 names against each other and `shapeGroups` joins any pair above a stated threshold — which is how the two look-alike pairs stopped being a judgement call: **fatha ~ kasra 0.968, fathatan ~ kasratan 0.914**, the largest unjoined cell 0.627, and the same grouping at every threshold from 0.70 to 0.90. `fitTo` matches width and height SEPARATELY, and that is not a detail: the comparison originally rescaled nothing, this print sizes a mark by what is under it (up to a third of its own width), and a multi-stroke mark compared against a differently-sized copy lands ink on gap and scores below zero. That produced 45 apparent mislabels which were all artefacts. The repair was chosen by competition against those 45 — ten-scale ladder 22, isotropic diagonal 32, widened window 24, separate axes **42**. `pieces`/`pieceCheck` score stroke-by-stroke, used to EXPLAIN a verdict and deliberately not to make one: arrangement is the only thing separating fathatan from successive fathatan.

One page of marks, read once and cached: the ligature corpus's own `<path data-diacritic>` boxes put onto our frame through `applierFromPin`, each carrying the surah, ayah and word index of the word it was drawn inside. Extracted from `probe-mark-ink.mjs` when a second consumer appeared, for the reason every other shared reader here exists: two walks over the same 380 MB cache is two chances to disagree about what a mark is, and the disagreement would show up as a placement finding. Wants the gitignored `data/pages/.cache/words/**`, which is why nothing that imports it can be a gate.

The trial plan a person works, and the reason their answers count as evidence: it is a pure function of the seed and the measured displacements, so no key is ever written to disk — the page holds none and the scorer rebuilds the same session afterwards. Four kinds, shuffled and indistinguishable while you work: **as shipped** (the corrected rectangle against the one the app draws today — the question), **decoy** (against the same distance in another direction, at least 30° off the as-shipped bearing; it is both the yardstick for whether an eye resolves a shift this small AND what breaks the pattern, since the error points the same way on every page and twenty trials is enough to learn that), **catch** (4.5 units off — anybody looking gets these, a session that fails them is discarded), **twin** (the same rectangle twice, where "can't tell" is the only honest answer, which is what catches a person who always picks something). Candidates are walked page-by-page in rotation rather than shuffled flat, because a flat shuffle over 40 pages of ~540 marks yields a session about four pages and the correction is per-page. Its readers are injected, not imported at the call site, so the arithmetic — the mix, the angles, the left/right balance — is testable on invented marks without the 380 MB cache.

The other plan, in the same module and deliberately not in the same session: no choosing, one rectangle, and a reader who drags it where it belongs. It exists because a forced choice yields at most one bit — *is ours preferred to what ships* — and a correction that points the right way and falls a third short wins every trial and is still wrong. Subtracting the machine's proposed move from the reader's landing gives the residual, which is a distance that can be applied rather than a preference that can only be counted. `START_R` puts every rectangle 3 units out in a uniformly random direction: well clear of both placements a forced choice would have offered (about 1 unit apart), so nobody lands by not moving; inside the window with the box's own half-width to spare; and evenly spread, so the pull a hand exerts toward its own starting point cancels in the average instead of being baked in as a fact about the boxes. `REPEAT_GAP` keeps a mark's two showings at least 10 trials apart, and those showings are inserted across the session rather than appended — the pair measures the reader's precision, and a precision built from the last fifteen trials measures the end of an hour. Placement cannot be offered inside a two-panel trial: dragging to fit and then comparing the landing to the two starts *is* the answer key, and offering the drag after the answer leaks the correction's direction across the session.

Which pages a sitting is allowed to draw from, and the answer to the largest limitation the first two sittings had: every trial they offered came from one of the forty pages the correction had been fitted to, so neither could ever have said the correction *travels*. `exclude` holds out the pages an earlier sitting used; `pages` says how many to keep. The keeping is deliberately not random — it takes from both ends of the spread on each axis, then the pages furthest from the middle of both, because what makes the SIZE of the correction readable is leverage and not sample size: across the original forty the proposed moves spanned about a third of a unit, nearly all of it measurement noise, and no number of placements on pages that all want the same move can separate a correction that is right from one that is a fifth short. Across the held-out forty the same span is 1.75 across and 3.38 down. The chosen list is written into the session and **replayed** when it is scored rather than recomputed here — the scorer rebuilds its trial list from the seed, so a narrowing applied at build time and not at score time would put every trial index against a different mark with nothing throwing, and recomputing instead of replaying would mean any later improvement to this function silently re-scores every sitting ever banked. Order is preserved for the same reason the seed is: the planner shuffles the array it is handed, so the same pages in a different order are a different session. It keeps a second strategy, `even`, and the two exist because the two sittings estimate different kinds of thing from the same pages. A placing session reads a slope off a regression, and a slope is bought with leverage, so it wants the ends of the range and does not mind that they are unusual pages. A forced choice reports a proportion — how often a reader prefers ours — and a proportion has no leverage to gain and a representativeness to lose: ask it only about the extremes and it fills with the easiest trials and the impossible ones, then reports the result as a fact about the mus'haf. `even` is a systematic every-k-th walk through the print rather than a random draw, for the same reason nothing here has a second seed: the same inputs must give the same list on any engine months later. The half-step offset keeps it off both ends, and consecutive indices are at least one apart by construction, so no page is named twice.

What has to match before two sittings may be compared with each other, and it lives beside the planners because they are what defines a build: the same seed, the same length, the same displacements and the same page list produce the same trials in the same order from the same starting points, and any one of them differing means the two people were not asked the same question. It returns every mismatch rather than the first, because a wrong file is usually wrong in several ways at once and being told about them one run at a time is how somebody gives up and averages the two anyway. The fifth check is the one worth writing down: two sittings that agree on all four of those *and* on who sat them is one hand compared against itself, which returns beautiful agreement, answers nothing, and — unlike a wrong-build comparison — leaves nothing in the printed output that would look odd to a reader.

Renders the session to one self-contained page: two panels, one rectangle each, no verdict, no feedback, no answers in the payload. `panel` is its own renderer and must stay that way — the measurement's own crop draws the other printing's outline in green exactly where the corrected rectangle goes, which is the answer key in a colour. Every panel is the same fixed square window (`windowFor`) plus a small framing wobble, so a catch cannot be spotted by its zoom and the corrected box is never dead centre. Asks a second question alongside the first — a tick, `N`, for *neither rectangle closes around the mark* — and it is a tick rather than a fourth button on purpose: a box can be in the right place and the wrong size, which is a different fault with a different repair, and a single "wrong somehow" answer would both blend the two and eat the trials where "which is closer" still has an answer. `head.asks` records that the question was put, so a ruling worked before it existed scores as *not asked* rather than as nobody-complained. Fingerprints the displacement file into the page so a ruling can be refused later if the measurement moved underneath it. Since the full 604-page pass it takes `--exclude` and `--pages` too, handed to `selectPages` with `even` as its default rather than the placing session's `extremes`, and for the reason that function's own note gives: this page only ever asks which of two rectangles is closer, so it estimates nothing from how far apart the proposed moves are and would only lose by bunching at the ends. The narrowing is what the check that releases the mark layer actually needed — until the measurement covered 604 pages, every question this page could ask came from one of the forty the correction was fitted to, so a hundred trials bought a very precise answer about training pages. The page list it settles on goes into the head with its own fingerprint, is replayed rather than recomputed when the ruling is scored, and is folded into both the localStorage key and the name of the file that lands in your downloads — two sittings from one seed that asked about different pages would otherwise share a resume key and stack one's answers onto the other's trials, and arrive in the same folder under the same name.
